children.value: The previous two sections produced a long list of signals: BM25F over several fields, proximity, anchor text, PageRank, site quality, location, and language. A real search engine adds many more, such as freshness, the URL depth, the share of users who clicked a page for similar queries, or the score of a neural reranker. Google has long described its ranking as built from hundreds of signals. All of them must be combined into one score per page, and the combination decides what the user sees.

This section starts with an example that combines four signals by hand and asks how to find the best combination. It then formalizes the question as a machine learning problem with three parts: the training data, the scoring model, and the loss. Finally, it shows how the models are trained and how search engines keep collecting the labels for training, mainly from the clicks of their users. The section closes with feeds, which use the same machinery to rank content without any query.
No search engine applies its most expensive ranking function to billions of pages. Ranking happens in stages, and each stage hands a smaller candidate set to a more expensive model, as
shows. The retriever uses the inverted index (

) and a cheap score such as BM25F to select on the order of ten thousand candidates. For each candidate, the system computes the full feature vector. A learned ranker, typically an ensemble of gradient-boosted decision trees, orders the candidates. A neural reranker, such as a cross-encoder (
), rescores the top hundred. Finally, the result page is composed from the ranked list and other elements such as ads and knowledge panels (

children.alt: The web ranking stack: each stage passes fewer candidates to a more expensive model.

children.value: Adding proximity does not help, since the three pages that matter score almost the same on it. Adding PageRank or anchor text fixes the ranking. But three quite different weight vectors are now perfect, including one that uses the anchor text alone. This query cannot tell them apart. Other queries can: anchor text alone fails for a new page that nobody links to yet, and a high PageRank weight pushes strong home pages to the top even for queries that they match only weakly.

A good weight vector must therefore work on average over thousands of queries at once. It must cover hundreds of signals, not four, and it must be chosen again whenever the signals or the web change. Tuning by hand does not scale to this. Instead, we collect queries with judged candidates and let an algorithm search for the weights that rank them best.

The three families trade expressiveness against cost and transparency. Tree ensembles are the strongest choice for hand-crafted features such as those in our table, and they sit in the middle of the ranking stack. Cross-encoders are the most expressive, but also the most expensive, so they only rescore the top candidates.

Pointwise, pairwise, listwise: what is the training example?

The three families are not model types. Any of the scoring models above (a linear function, trees, or a neural network) can be trained with any of the three losses. What differs is the unit of training and the loss: one document and its grade (pointwise), one pair and its order (pairwise), or one whole result list and its nDCG (listwise).

Trees cannot be trained by gradient descent on their parameters, since their thresholds and leaf values do not change smoothly.

(LambdaRank trained with decision trees) combines the lambda weights with MART (multiple additive regression trees), a form of gradient-boosted decision trees. LambdaRank defines what to optimize: the lambdas. MART defines how the model grows: each new tree is fitted to the lambdas of the current ensemble, so the ensemble grows in the direction that improves nDCG most. LambdaMART won the Yahoo! Learning to Rank Challenge in 2010 and remains a strong baseline for ranking over many hand-crafted features. Libraries such as LightGBM and XGBoost implement it with a

Gradient-boosted trees over hand-crafted features dominated web ranking in the 2000s and early 2010s. Since 2019, transformer models have taken over a growing part of the stack. Google announced in 2019 that it uses BERT to understand queries and rank results, affecting about one in ten English queries in the US at launch. A cross-encoder reads query and page together and captures meaning that no feature vector expresses, for example that “can you get medicine for someone pharmacy” is about picking up a prescription for another person. Neural rankers have not replaced learning to rank; they have joined it. A neural reranker is trained with the same pointwise, pairwise, or listwise losses, often on the same mix of human labels and clicks. Its output can become one more feature for a tree ensemble, or the final stage of the stack in
Example: Learning to rank on TREC-COVID

has 50 topics with 66,336 graded judgments. We take the judged papers of each topic as its candidate list and describe each topic-paper pair by eight features: BM25 on title and abstract, BM25F, proximity, the fraction of query terms present, the two field lengths, and the cosine similarity of sentence embeddings as a neural score. Each ranker is trained on 40 topics and evaluated on the other 10, in five rounds, with features normalized per topic:

Every ranker that learns from all eight features beats the best single signal. Within each model family, the pairwise or listwise loss beats the pointwise one, and LambdaMART is best overall. Without per-topic normalization, the trees lose this lead (LambdaMART 0.789). The last row shows that the neural score does not replace the term statistics but completes them: without it, the remaining features are variants of the same term counts and add nothing over BM25F. On 50 topics, differences of about 0.01 are within the noise.

A ranker is never trained only once. New pages appear, events create new queries, the meaning of queries shifts, and every new signal requires a new model. Search engines therefore retrain their rankers regularly, and they need a steady supply of fresh labels. Two sources provide them.

judge query-page pairs on a graded scale, following detailed guidelines. Their labels are precise and reflect the intended notion of quality, but they are slow and expensive. Search engines therefore spend them where precision matters most: on test sets that evaluate every new ranker offline with nDCG (
), and on hard or new kinds of queries.

is the second source: which results users click, how long they stay on the clicked page, and whether they return to the result list to try another result. Clicks are abundant and free, and they reflect the needs of real users rather than the opinion of raters. Every day of traffic adds millions of new examples. They are also heavily biased.

. Users click the top results much more often, partly because they are better, but mostly because they are on top. In an eye-tracking study, Joachims et al. swapped the first two results without telling the users, and the result at rank 1 still received most clicks. A click on rank 1 is weak evidence of relevance; a click on rank 5 is strong evidence, since the user read past four other results to get there. Joachims’s early solution used clicks to create pairwise preferences: if the user skipped the result at rank 2 and clicked the one at rank 3, then

A click shows that a result looked promising in the result list, not that the page satisfied the user. Attractive titles and thumbnails earn clicks regardless of quality, which rewards clickbait. Search engines therefore use refined signals: long dwell time on the clicked page counts as success, while a quick return to the result list (a “pogo-stick” back to the results) counts as failure. Even so, a model trained on clicks optimizes what users click, which is not always what is good for them. We meet this tension again in
Clicks also decide whether a new ranker goes live. Offline metrics on a judged test set cannot capture everything. Search engines therefore run online experiments: an
shows the new ranker to a small fraction of users and compares click and satisfaction metrics with the current one.
mixes the results of both rankers into one list and checks which ranker’s results attract more clicks; it needs far fewer users than an A/B test to detect a difference.

Together, these steps form a loop. The deployed ranker produces result pages, the result pages produce clicks, the debiased clicks train the next ranker, and online experiments decide whether it replaces the current one. The loop has a blind spot: users can only click what the ranker shows, so a page that never reaches the first result page never collects the clicks it would need to get there. The randomized swaps that estimate propensities also help here, since they show some results at positions where the current ranker would not put them. The same staged design and the same loop also power recommendation feeds, which we turn to next.

Open TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, or X, and the app shows content before the user types anything. Every swipe asks the same question as a search engine: of the hundreds of millions of items available right now, which few should this user see next? The weights of the sum are a product decision, not a learned quantity, and they decide what the feed becomes. X, which published the source code of its home timeline in 2023, weighted a like with 0.5, a reply with 13.5, and a reply that the post’s author engages with 75. Such weights favour conversations; high weights on shares or watch time favour content that spreads. The warning about clicks applies here with full force. Replies, shares, and watch time correlate with interest, but outrage and sensational content produce them as well. A feed trained purely on engagement can amplify divisive content and narrow what a user sees into a
. Platforms counter this with negative feedback signals, quality classifiers, diversity rules, and surveys that ask users directly whether a post was worth their time.
Feeds also face sharper versions of the evaluation problems of web search. The log only shows reactions to what the current system chose to show, so a feed reserves part of its slots for

, such as new creators and new topics, to learn anything new about its users. And since there is no ground truth for which post a user should have seen, feeds are evaluated almost entirely online, with A/B tests that track long-term effects such as whether users return next week, not only short-term engagement. Search and feeds thus share the same end point: both learn to rank from user behaviour, and both must keep the measured behaviour from replacing the goal it stands for.
